_what: The exemption register RFC-2026-016 §4 made the replacement for "force RLS where compatible".
_why: "Where compatible" was retired for being unfalsifiable: no artefact could be pointed at to decide whether a table met it. A register is the falsifiable form -- an exemption either has a row here or it does not exist.

It is read in BOTH directions, which is what makes it a control rather than a list. A table that is not forced and has no row is refused. A row whose exemption is not visible in the catalog is refused too, because a register that keeps rows for exemptions nobody took is a register nobody can trust to be complete.

It was mandated on 2026-09-05 and did not exist until 2026-09-06. A1's countersignature §5.1 found the gap: the phrase was retired for being unfalsifiable and its replacement was unfalsifiable by absence.

_shape.role: the role the exemption is for -- a role name, or "*" when the exemption is the table not being forced at all
_shape.table: unqualified table name in the app schema
_shape.reason: why the general rule cannot hold here, in a sentence someone can disagree with
_shape.owner: the run or human accountable for removing it
_shape.review_date: ISO date. An exemption past its review date is a finding, not a grandfathered fact.

_what_the_catalog_can_corroborate: The shape above is the RFC's. What db/foundation/lint/catalog-snapshot.json can CORROBORATE is narrower, and the lint enforces the narrower thing rather than declaring the wider one. C0's review D2 found the granularity declared and unenforced: a row scoped to one role and one operation was matched to its table by name alone and bought that table a blanket pass.

role "*" is a claim about the TABLE. relforcerowsecurity is one value for the whole table -- every role and every operation at once -- so this is the only scope an unforced table corroborates, and the only scope that suppresses the unforced-table finding. It requires operation "all".

A named role is a claim about the ROLE. rolbypassrls and rolsuper hold for every table at once, so such a row is checked against that role's own attributes, and naming a table in it narrows nothing. It suppresses no table finding, because a table's FORCE state is not evidence about a role.

An operation other than "all" is refused. No field in the snapshot says which command a policy is for, so a per-operation exemption can be corroborated in neither direction -- the same unfalsifiable shape "where compatible" was retired for.

rls_enabled is not exemptible at all. RFC-2026-012 commits the whole client/database boundary to row level security; §4 retired only the FORCE condition, and this register replaces that condition and nothing else.
